question:
During a classroom investigation, students use the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3\\1 & 0 & 2\\4 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ to study how elementary row operations affect a determinant. They obtain a second matrix $B$ by interchanging the first two rows of $A$, multiplying the third row by $3$, and then adding twice the first row of the resulting matrix to its second row. The students want to predict the determinant of $B$ without expanding it completely and then confirm their prediction.

(a) Evaluate $|A|$.

(b) Predict $|B|$ using the effects of the stated row operations.

(c) Construct $B$ and verify its determinant by direct expansion.

(d) Justify whether both matrices are non-singular.
explanation:
(a)
Expanding along the first row,
$$|A|=2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2\\1 & 5\end{vmatrix}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2\\4 & 5\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0\\4 & 1\end{vmatrix}$$
$$|A|=2(0-2)-(5-8)+3(1-0)$$
$$|A|=-4+3+3=2$$

(b)
Interchanging two rows changes the sign of the determinant, so the determinant becomes $-2$. Multiplying the third row by $3$ multiplies the determinant by $3$, giving $-6$. Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant. Therefore,
$$|B|=-6$$

(c)
After interchanging the first two rows,
$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2\\2 & 1 & 3\\4 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}$$
Multiplying the third row by $3$ and then applying $R_2\to R_2+2R_1$ gives
$$B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2\\4 & 1 & 7\\12 & 3 & 15\end{bmatrix}$$
Expanding along the first row,
$$|B|=1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 7\\3 & 15\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1\\12 & 3\end{vmatrix}$$
$$|B|=(15-21)+2(12-12)=-6$$
Thus, the predicted value is verified.

(d)
A square matrix is non-singular when its determinant is non-zero. Since
$$|A|=2\neq0\quad\text{and}\quad|B|=-6\neq0$$
both $A$ and $B$ are non-singular.

options.D:
(a) $|A|=2$
(b) $|B|=-6$
(c) $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2\\2&1&3\\12&3&15\end{bmatrix}$ and $|B|=-6$
(d) $A$ is non-singular but $B$ is singular
